positions/historic-premillennialism/oneL: After a final tribulation the Church will meet the returning Christ, who will raise the righteous and reign on earth for a thousand years before the last judgement and new creation.
positions/historic-premillennialism/core: Revelation 19–20 is sequential: Christ returns (ch. 19), then reigns with resurrected saints for a thousand years (ch. 20), then the final judgement.
There are two bodily resurrections: of the righteous at Christ’s coming, and of the rest after the millennium.
The Church passes through the great tribulation; the rapture and the visible second coming are one event (posttribulational).
The Church is the one people of God in continuity with faithful Israel, though many expect a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ (Rom 11:25–26).
The millennium vindicates God’s good creation and the body by renewing this earth.
positions/historic-premillennialism/orig: The earliest attested Christian eschatology after the New Testament: Papias (c.110), Justin Martyr (c.155), Irenaeus (c.180), Tertullian, Hippolytus, Lactantius and Commodian, drawing on Jewish apocalyptic hopes for a messianic age. Eclipsed by Augustine in the West and by Origenist spiritual exegesis in the East, it revived among 17th-century scholars (Joseph Mede, 1627) and in the 19th-century prophetic movement, and was given modern scholarly form by George Eldon Ladd.
positions/historic-premillennialism/stro: It is the most natural reading of Revelation 19–20 as narrative sequence, and of "they came to life" (ezesan) as bodily resurrection in both verses 4 and 5.
It is the earliest documented post-apostolic view, held by figures in direct contact with the apostolic generation (Papias, via the "elders who saw John").
Paul’s order "Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming. Then cometh the end" (1 Cor 15:23–24) leaves room for an interval.
It honours the material, this-worldly character of the prophetic promises without needing the Israel/Church dualism of dispensationalism.
Revelation 20 is the only text to mention a millennium; building an entire era on one passage in a highly symbolic book is precarious.
It introduces an awkward mixed world of glorified saints and mortal sinners on earth after Christ’s return, which the rest of the New Testament never describes.
Early chiliasm was not universal (Justin concedes this) and was associated with sensual expectations Origen and Eusebius found sub-Christian.
Confessional churches (Augsburg XVII; Catholic Holy Office 1944) explicitly rejected it.
positions/historic-premillennialism/resp: Premillennialists reply that a doctrine taught once in inspired Scripture is still taught; and the millennium makes sense of many Old Testament texts about long life and peace on a still-mortal earth (Isa 65:20).
The confessional condemnations were aimed chiefly at violent or carnal chiliasm (Münster), not at the sober premillennialism of Irenaeus.
Origen’s alternative imported Platonic suspicion of the body, which the creeds’ "resurrection of the flesh" itself resists.
positions/historic-premillennialism/cons: Gave the second-century Church a robust theology of creation and bodily resurrection against Gnosticism.
Persists as a non-dispensational option in evangelical scholarship and in many Global South churches.
Provided the base from which dispensationalism developed and against which it is often measured.
positions/dispensational-premillennialis: Dispensational premillennialism

Darbyism (critics)

God works through successive "dispensations" and keeps distinct purposes for Israel and the Church: the Church will be raptured before a seven-year tribulation, after which Christ returns to rule a literal thousand-year kingdom centred on a restored Israel.
Scripture should be read with a consistently "literal" (grammatical-historical) hermeneutic, including prophecy.
Israel and the Church are distinct peoples of God; the Church is a "mystery" parenthesis not foreseen by the prophets.
God’s unconditional covenants with Abraham and David guarantee ethnic Israel a land and kingdom yet to be fulfilled.
Daniel’s seventieth "week" (Dan 9:27) is a future seven-year tribulation; the Church is removed before it (pretribulation rapture).
Christ returns after the tribulation to rule from Jerusalem for a literal thousand years.
History is divided into dispensations (classically seven: innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom).

Formulated by the Anglo-Irish former clergyman John Nelson Darby (1800–1882) of the Plymouth Brethren in the late 1820s and early 1830s, partly through the Powerscourt prophecy conferences (1831–33) and amid wider British prophetic excitement (Edward Irving; Lacunza’s futurism). Spread in North America by Darby’s preaching tours (1862–77), the Niagara Bible Conferences (from 1878), D. L. Moody’s circle, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and Dallas Theological Seminary (1924). Later forms: "revised" (Ryrie, Walvoord) and "progressive" dispensationalism (Blaising and Bock, 1990s).

Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock (progressive)
A consistent literal hermeneutic protects prophecy from subjective allegorising: if God promised land to Abraham’s descendants "for ever" (Gen 13:15), God’s faithfulness requires it.
Paul insists "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance" and that "all Israel shall be saved" (Rom 11:26–29), indicating a future for ethnic Israel.
Texts promising deliverance "from the wrath to come" (1 Thess 1:10; 5:9; Rev 3:10) and the imminence of Christ’s coming best fit a rapture before the tribulation.
It gives a coherent, teachable framework for the whole Bible and has proven remarkably fruitful in evangelism, Bible teaching and missions.
Historical novelty: no clear pretribulation rapture or two-peoples ecclesiology appears in the Church’s first 1,800 years.
The New Testament treats the Church as the fulfilment of Israel’s hope, one "new man" of Jews and Gentiles (Eph 2:14–16; Gal 3:29; 1 Pet 2:9), not a parenthesis.

The "literal hermeneutic" is applied selectively (e.g. to the 1,000 years but not to the seven-headed beast), and the New Testament itself reads Old Testament prophecy typologically (Acts 2:16–21; 15:15–18).

Critics, including Palestinian Christians, argue it fosters date-setting speculation and uncritical political support for the State of Israel, and diminishes concern for the present world ("you don’t polish brass on a sinking ship").
Dispensationalists answer that the recovery of neglected truth is a Reformation principle, and that early chiliasm and imminence-language (e.g. Pseudo-Ephraem) contain the seeds of the view.
Progressive dispensationalists concede more continuity between Israel and the Church (one people, distinct roles) and an "already/not yet" kingdom, softening the sharpest dichotomies.

Leading scholars (Walvoord, Bock) explicitly reject date-setting, and many dispensationalists support Palestinian Christian ministries; political support for Israel is not entailed by the theology alone.
Became the dominant eschatology of 20th-century American fundamentalism, much of Pentecostalism and of evangelical missions worldwide.
Generated a vast popular literature and media industry: The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), A Thief in the Night (1972 film), Left Behind (1995–2007).
Shaped American Christian Zionism and evangelical attitudes to the Middle East.
Its Bible-institute network (Moody, Dallas, Biola) trained generations of pastors and missionaries.
positions/pretribulation-rapture/oneLine: Christ will come for his Church, catching living believers up to meet him in the air, before a seven-year tribulation; he will return with them at its end.
positions/pretribulation-rapture/coreCla: The rapture (1 Thess 4:16–17) and the visible second coming (Rev 19) are two distinct events separated by the tribulation.
The rapture is imminent: it can occur at any moment, with no prophesied signs preceding it.
The tribulation is the outpouring of God’s wrath and Daniel’s seventieth week, concerning Israel; the Church is "not appointed to wrath" (1 Thess 5:9).
The Church is absent from Revelation 4–19 on earth, suggesting it has been removed.
The restrainer of 2 Thessalonians 2:7 is the Holy Spirit indwelling the Church, removed at the rapture.
positions/pretribulation-rapture/origin: Developed by J. N. Darby c.1827–1833 in the Brethren movement and widely popularised via Scofield and Bible conferences. Its origin is debated: claims that it came from a vision of the Scottish teenager Margaret Macdonald (1830) or from Edward Irving’s circle are contested; advocates point to partial precedents in Pseudo-Ephraem (a Latin sermon, c.4th–7th century), Morgan Edwards (1788) and Increase Mather.
positions/pretribulation-rapture/propone: Many Pentecostal and Baptist confessions (e.g. Assemblies of God "blessed hope")
positions/pretribulation-rapture/stronge: Only a pretribulational rapture preserves genuine imminence: believers are told to watch for Christ, not for the Antichrist or tribulation signs (Titus 2:13; James 5:8).
The promise to keep the church "from (ek) the hour of temptation which shall come upon all the world" (Rev 3:10) implies removal from the period itself.
If the righteous were raptured at the end of the tribulation, no mortal believers would remain to enter and populate the millennium.
Distinguishing features: at the rapture Christ comes "for" his saints in the air; at the second coming he comes "with" them to the earth (Zech 14:4; Jude 14).
Absence from the historical Church before c.1830 (Pseudo-Ephraem is disputed and ambiguous).
Paul says the "day of the Lord" will not come until the man of sin is revealed (2 Thess 2:1–4), linking the "gathering together unto him" to that day, after Antichrist.
The same Greek words (parousia, apokalypsis, epiphaneia) are used for the coming of Christ in "rapture" and "second coming" texts alike; no text explicitly describes two future comings.
"Meet" (apantēsis, 1 Thess 4:17) was used of citizens going out to escort a visiting dignitary back into the city, suggesting believers rise to accompany Christ to earth, not to depart with him.
positions/pretribulation-rapture/respons: Pretribulationists reply that 2 Thess 2:3 can be read "unless the departure (apostasia) comes first", i.e. the rapture itself; others argue the "day of the Lord" begins with the tribulation and the Thessalonians feared they had missed the rapture.
Shared vocabulary does not prove a single event; context distinguishes them, as Old Testament prophecy merged the two comings of Christ that the New Testament distinguishes.
The lack of early explicit statements reflects the undeveloped state of eschatology, not a refutation; the early Church did hold imminence.
positions/pretribulation-rapture/consequ: Generated the most famous popular images of modern evangelical eschatology: empty clothes, driverless cars, Left Behind.
Fostered intense watchfulness and evangelistic urgency, and sometimes date-setting (e.g. Edgar Whisenant, 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988).
Encouraged the view that Christians will escape global catastrophe, criticised by some as fostering escapism.
